Customer data first. At Sotheby’s the CDP sat at the center of a stack that took organic traffic up 167%, and it worked because the whole stack worked together.

Douglas Cirillo was Assistant Vice President, Director of Digital Product and Growth Stack at Sotheby’s from 2017 to 2020. He directed the rearchitecture of Sotheby’s digital and growth stack, including the migration from Adobe Experience Manager onto a composable, data-first stack, running the function with one direct report and a vendor team of about 20, directing $5 to $6M in spend. Organic traffic rose 167%, search click-through rose 48.7%, consignment search placement doubled, and consignment ad spend fell 50%.

Read the case study

Composable martech is a stack built from best-of-breed tools, each chosen for one job and connected through defined interfaces, instead of a single vendor suite. The content platform, the data platform, the decisioning tools, and the analytics layer are separate components with clean contracts between them: documented schemas, stable interfaces, clear ownership. When one component stops earning its place, you can replace that component without rebuilding the whole stack, and you do not wait for a suite vendor’s roadmap to catch up with your business.

Digital experience strategy is the work of deciding what a brand’s website and apps should do, then building the team and the data to do it. The deliverable is not a deck. It is one set of metrics that matter, one shared understanding of the customer, and a sequence the organization can actually execute: what gets built, in what order, and how everyone will know it worked.

Technology decisions are only part of the strategy. The harder work is deciding what matters first, who owns it, what the organization can deliver, and how progress will be measured.

Every test names its objective and one primary metric before it runs, and results are reported in business currency. The scorecard is the diagnostic I use.

Experimentation is how an organization finds out whether a change worked. A test states a hypothesis, names one primary metric before it runs, and reads the result against that metric, which means the tests aim at a specific outcome and the decisioning is built to test against the objective, not the screen.

None of that holds without the layer underneath: events defined the same way by every team, metrics that mean the same thing in every dashboard, and readouts people trust enough to act on. Measurement is the precondition. Shared KPIs, shared language, governance and reporting, agreed before the tooling arguments start.

Gates, not prompts. A prompt is a request; a gate is a control.

The harness checks are Brand Out-of-Bounds, Contextual Switch, and Guardrails. A prompt is a request; a gate is a control.
